title: Ruby on Rails Tutorial Study Slides
description: Chapter-by-chapter code slides, method explanations, important Rails ideas, and an appendix for quick lookup.

chapters.title: From zero to deploy
chapters.theme: Rails app lifecycle, Bundler, server, MVC, Git, deployment

slides.title: Rails project boot sequence
slides.code:
gem install rails -v 6.0.3
rails _6.0.3_ new hello_app
cd hello_app
bundle install
rails server
slides.explanation: A Rails app starts as a generated directory structure. Bundler resolves Ruby gem dependencies, then `rails server` boots the Rack app so browser requests can reach Rails.

methods.name: rails new
methods.explanation: Generates a Rails application skeleton with app, config, db, test, and Gemfile directories.

methods.name: bundle install
methods.explanation: Installs exact gem versions needed by the application.

methods.name: rails server
methods.explanation: Starts the local web server for development.

important: Understand Rails as a request/response web framework.
Gemfile changes usually require `bundle install`.
Git should capture small working checkpoints before deployment.
slides.output: A local development server responds at a localhost URL and renders the default Rails page or custom app response.

chapters.title: A toy app
chapters.theme: Scaffolded resources, REST, MVC, generated Users and Microposts

slides.title: Resource scaffold and REST routes
slides.code:
rails generate scaffold User name:string email:string
rails generate scaffold Micropost content:text user_id:integer
rails db:migrate
resources :users
resources :microposts
slides.explanation: Scaffolding creates a quick CRUD resource across model, view, controller, routes, and migration. It is useful for seeing Rails conventions, but real apps usually replace scaffolded code with custom flows.

methods.name: resources
methods.explanation: Creates the standard RESTful routes: index, show, new, create, edit, update, destroy.

methods.name: db:migrate
methods.explanation: Applies pending database schema changes from migration files.

methods.name: has_many / belongs_to
methods.explanation: Express model relationships and add association helper methods.

important: REST routes are central to Rails controller design.
Generated scaffolds demonstrate conventions but are not polished production UX.
Associations are more expressive than raw foreign-key handling.
slides.output: `/users` and `/microposts` expose CRUD screens backed by database tables.

chapters.title: Mostly static pages
chapters.theme: Controllers, views, routes, first tests, red/green/refactor

slides.title: Static controller and route-driven pages
slides.code:
rails generate controller StaticPages home help

# config/routes.rb
root 'static_pages#home'
get '/help', to: 'static_pages#help'
slides.explanation: Static pages are still routed through controllers. The route decides which controller action runs, then Rails renders the matching view template unless told otherwise.

methods.name: root
methods.explanation: Defines the homepage route.

methods.name: get
methods.explanation: Maps a GET request path to a controller action.

methods.name: assert_select
methods.explanation: Checks rendered HTML in Rails integration/controller tests.

important: Testing page titles catches routing and template regressions.
Rails defaults to implicit rendering when action and template names match.
Red/green/refactor gives a disciplined workflow for UI behavior.
slides.output: Visiting `/`, `/help`, and other static paths renders corresponding templates with testable HTML.

chapters.title: Rails-flavored Ruby
chapters.theme: Ruby strings, arrays, hashes, blocks, classes, helpers

slides.title: Helpers are Ruby methods used by views
slides.code:
module ApplicationHelper
  def full_title(page_title = '')
    base_title = 'Ruby on Rails Tutorial Sample App'
    if page_title.empty?
      base_title
    else
      "#{page_title} | #{base_title}"
    end
  end
end
slides.explanation: Rails helpers are ordinary Ruby methods made available to views. They keep templates focused on presentation while moving reusable formatting logic into Ruby.

methods.name: def
methods.explanation: Defines a Ruby method.

methods.name: empty?
methods.explanation: Predicate method that returns true if a string or collection has no content.

methods.name: interpolation
methods.explanation: `#{...}` inserts Ruby expression results into a string.

important: Rails code reads naturally because Ruby allows expressive method names.
Blocks power many Rails APIs.
Symbols and hashes appear constantly in routes, validations, and options.
slides.output: `full_title('Help')` returns `Help | Ruby on Rails Tutorial Sample App`.

chapters.title: Filling in the layout
chapters.theme: Layout, partials, asset pipeline, named routes, signup URL

slides.title: Named routes make links resilient
slides.code:
# config/routes.rb
root 'static_pages#home'
get '/help',    to: 'static_pages#help'
get '/signup',  to: 'users#new'

# app/views/layouts/application.html.erb
<%= link_to 'Home', root_path %>
<%= link_to 'Sign up', signup_path %>
slides.explanation: Named route helpers decouple view links from raw URL strings. If a path changes in routes, templates can keep using semantic helpers.

methods.name: link_to
methods.explanation: Generates an HTML anchor tag.

methods.name: root_path
methods.explanation: URL helper generated by the `root` route.

methods.name: render
methods.explanation: Renders a partial or template into the current view.

important: Partials reduce duplicated header/footer/link markup.
The asset pipeline organizes stylesheets, JavaScript, and images.
Named routes are safer than hard-coded URL strings.
slides.output: The layout renders reusable navigation links that point to current route definitions.

chapters.title: Modeling users
chapters.theme: Active Record, migrations, validations, secure password

slides.title: User model validations and secure password
slides.explanation: Active Record models combine database persistence with domain rules. Validations prevent bad records, callbacks normalize data, and `has_secure_password` wires password hashing and authentication.

methods.name: validates
methods.explanation: Declares validation rules checked before saving.

methods.name: before_save
methods.explanation: Runs code before a record is persisted.

methods.name: has_secure_password
methods.explanation: Adds password digest handling and `authenticate`.

important: Database constraints and model validations should complement each other.
Email uniqueness needs case normalization plus a unique database index.
Never store raw passwords.
slides.output: Invalid users fail `valid?`; valid users can be saved and later authenticated.

chapters.title: Sign up
chapters.theme: User resource, form_with, strong parameters, flash, signup tests

slides.title: Strong parameters protect mass assignment
slides.code:
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @user = User.new(user_params)
    if @user.save
      flash[:success] = 'Welcome to the Sample App!'
      redirect_to @user
    else
      render 'new'
    end
  end

  private

  def user_params
    params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :password, :password_confirmation)
  end
end
slides.explanation: The controller creates a user only from permitted fields. Successful signup redirects and stores a flash message; failed signup renders the form again with validation errors.

methods.name: params.require
methods.explanation: Requires a top-level parameter key.

methods.name: permit
methods.explanation: Allows only listed attributes through mass assignment.

methods.name: flash
methods.explanation: Stores a message for the next rendered request or redirect.

important: Strong parameters are a core Rails security boundary.
`render` keeps the same request; `redirect_to` starts a new request.
Signup tests should cover both invalid and valid submissions.
slides.output: A valid POST creates a user and redirects to `/users/:id`; invalid data re-renders signup.

chapters.title: Basic login
chapters.theme: Sessions, login form, authenticate, current_user, logout

slides.title: Session-based login
slides.code:
module SessionsHelper
  def log_in(user)
    session[:user_id] = user.id
  end

  def current_user
    @current_user ||= User.find_by(id: session[:user_id])
  end

  def logged_in?
    !current_user.nil?
  end
end
slides.explanation: A Rails session stores a signed user id in the browser. `current_user` memoizes the database lookup so repeated calls during one request do not keep querying.

methods.name: session
methods.explanation: Per-browser signed data suitable for login state.

methods.name: find_by
methods.explanation: Returns the first matching record or nil.
Memoizes by assigning only when the left side is nil or false.

important: Use `flash.now` when rendering a failed login form, not `flash`.
Login state belongs in sessions, not hidden form fields.
Logout should delete the session user id.
slides.output: After login, helpers can answer who the current user is and whether layout links should change.

chapters.title: Advanced login
chapters.theme: Remember me, persistent cookies, token digest, subtle login bugs

slides.title: Persistent login with remember token
slides.code:
def remember(user)
  user.remember
  cookies.permanent.signed[:user_id] = user.id
  cookies.permanent[:remember_token] = user.remember_token
end

def forget(user)
  user.forget
  cookies.delete(:user_id)
  cookies.delete(:remember_token)
end
slides.explanation: Remember-me login uses persistent cookies plus a server-side token digest. The raw token goes to the browser; the digest stays in the database for comparison.

methods.name: cookies.permanent
methods.explanation: Stores a browser cookie with a long expiration.

methods.name: signed
methods.explanation: Prevents client-side tampering with cookie values.

methods.name: authenticated?
methods.explanation: Compares a token with a stored digest.

important: Treat remember tokens like passwords.
Clearing cookies and database digest must stay in sync.
Guard against nil digest bugs when users log out in multiple browsers.
slides.output: The user remains logged in across browser restarts until `forget` clears the persistent state.

chapters.title: Updating, showing, and deleting users
chapters.theme: Edit/update, authorization, before_action, friendly forwarding, pagination, admin destroy

slides.title: Authorization with before_action
slides.code:
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  before_action :logged_in_user, only: [:index, :edit, :update, :destroy]
  before_action :correct_user,   only: [:edit, :update]
  before_action :admin_user,     only: :destroy

  def correct_user
    @user = User.find(params[:id])
    redirect_to(root_url) unless current_user?(@user)
  end
end
slides.explanation: `before_action` centralizes access control so protected actions cannot run until required checks pass. Authorization is separate from authentication: logged in is not the same as allowed.

methods.name: before_action
methods.explanation: Runs filters before selected controller actions.

methods.name: current_user?
methods.explanation: Checks whether a given user equals the logged-in user.

methods.name: redirect_to
methods.explanation: Stops normal rendering and sends the browser to another URL.

important: Every write action needs authorization checks.
Friendly forwarding stores the intended URL before login.
Admin-only delete behavior should be tested.
slides.output: Wrong users are redirected away; admins can delete users; normal users cannot.

chapters.title: Account activation
chapters.theme: Activation tokens, mailers, account activation resource, authenticated? generalization

slides.title: Token-based account activation
slides.code:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  attr_accessor :activation_token
  before_create :create_activation_digest

  def create_activation_digest
    self.activation_token = User.new_token
    self.activation_digest = User.digest(activation_token)
  end
end
slides.explanation: Activation uses a temporary token emailed to the user and a digest stored in the database. The app verifies the token before marking the account activated.

methods.name: attr_accessor
methods.explanation: Creates a virtual attribute not persisted directly to the database.

methods.name: before_create
methods.explanation: Runs only before a new record is first saved.

methods.name: deliver_now
methods.explanation: Sends an email immediately through Action Mailer.

important: Email links should carry a token, not a password.
Store digests rather than raw tokens.
Only activated users should be allowed to log in.
slides.output: A signup creates an inactive user, sends email, and activation flips the account to active.

chapters.title: Password reset
chapters.theme: Reset tokens, reset emails, expiration, update password flow

slides.title: Password reset expiration
slides.code:
def create_reset_digest
  self.reset_token = User.new_token
  update_columns(reset_digest: User.digest(reset_token), reset_sent_at: Time.zone.now)
end

def password_reset_expired?
  reset_sent_at < 2.hours.ago
end
slides.explanation: Password reset works like account activation but adds a time window. Expiring old reset links limits damage from leaked emails or stale tokens.

methods.name: update_columns
methods.explanation: Updates database columns directly, bypassing validations and callbacks.

methods.name: Time.zone.now
methods.explanation: Uses Rails time zone awareness instead of system time.

methods.name: 2.hours.ago
methods.explanation: ActiveSupport time helper for readable duration logic.

important: Reset links should expire.
Blank password updates need special handling.
Reset tokens should be digested like activation and remember tokens.
slides.output: A valid recent token allows password update; an expired token redirects with an error.

chapters.title: User microposts
chapters.theme: Micropost model, dependent destroy, feed, image upload, validations

slides.title: User-owned microposts and feed basics
slides.code:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :microposts, dependent: :destroy
end

class Micropost < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :user
  default_scope -> { order(created_at: :desc) }
  validates :user_id, presence: true
  validates :content, presence: true, length: { maximum: 140 }
end
slides.explanation: Microposts belong to users, and a user owns many microposts. `dependent: :destroy` prevents orphaned posts, and `default_scope` makes newest posts appear first.

methods.name: has_many
methods.explanation: Defines one-to-many association methods.

methods.name: belongs_to
methods.explanation: Defines the inverse association and foreign-key expectation.

methods.name: default_scope
methods.explanation: Adds a default ordering or condition to model queries.

important: Always protect user-owned content with access control.
Dependent destroy is useful but can have performance implications.
Upload validation should restrict size and content type.
slides.output: `user.microposts` returns that user's posts, ordered newest first.

chapters.title: Following users
chapters.theme: Relationship model, has_many through, member routes, Ajax follow forms, status feed

slides.title: Following with has_many through
slides.code:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :active_relationships, class_name: 'Relationship', foreign_key: 'follower_id', dependent: :destroy
  has_many :passive_relationships, class_name: 'Relationship', foreign_key: 'followed_id', dependent: :destroy
  has_many :following, through: :active_relationships, source: :followed
  has_many :followers, through: :passive_relationships, source: :follower

  def follow(other_user)
    following << other_user
  end
end
slides.explanation: The follow graph is a self-referential relationship between users. Rails needs explicit class names, foreign keys, and source names to understand both sides.

methods.name: has_many :through
methods.explanation: Builds an association through a join model.

methods.name: class_name
methods.explanation: Tells Rails which model class to use when the association name is not enough.

methods.name: source
methods.explanation: Identifies the target association on the join model.

important: Following/followers is not a simple one-column association.
Uniqueness indexes prevent duplicate follows.
Feed queries are where app correctness and database performance meet.
slides.output: `user.following` returns users followed by `user`; `user.followers` returns users following `user`.
